questions.prompt: What is the core trade-off of adopting microservices?

options.text: They are always faster to build than a monolith
They enable independent scaling, deployment, and team autonomy, but impose full distributed-systems complexity
They remove the need for databases
They guarantee higher performance

questions.explanation: Microservices buy independence (scaling, deploys, tech, teams) at the price of network calls, partial failure, eventual consistency, and operational overhead.

questions.prompt: How should you draw microservice boundaries?

options.text: By technical layer (a database service, a logic service)
Around business capabilities / bounded contexts, with each service owning its own data
Randomly, to spread load
One service per database table

questions.explanation: Boundaries should follow business capabilities (bounded contexts), and each service should own its data so services can evolve independently.

options.text: A very large single application
Services so tightly coupled that they must be deployed together or share a database — the worst of both worlds
A monolith deployed to many servers
A microservice with its own database

questions.explanation: A distributed monolith has the operational cost of microservices and the coupling of a monolith: coupled deploys, shared databases, and long synchronous chains.

questions.prompt: Why do many experts recommend starting with a monolith?

options.text: Monoliths always outperform microservices
You don't yet know the right boundaries, premature splitting locks in wrong ones, and a good monolith scales far
Microservices are impossible to build
Monoliths never need to change

questions.explanation: Early on the correct service boundaries aren't clear; splitting too soon cements the wrong ones. A modular monolith scales a long way and can be extracted incrementally.

questions.prompt: What does Conway's Law imply for microservice design?

options.text: Services should be as small as possible
A system's structure mirrors the organization's communication structure, so align services with teams
All services must use the same language
Databases must be shared

questions.explanation: Conway's Law says system structure reflects org structure. Aligning service boundaries with team boundaries reduces coordination friction.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of the distributed-monolith anti-pattern? Select all that apply.

options.text: You can't deploy one service without deploying others
Multiple services share the same database tables
One request fans out through a long synchronous chain of services
Each service owns its own data and deploys independently

questions.explanation: Coupled deploys, shared databases, and long synchronous chains are the smells. Independent data ownership and deployment is the opposite — the healthy pattern.
